claims: AS-202 is often referred to as Apollo 2.
AS-202 was a successful uncrewed suborbital test flight of the Apollo command and service module.
AS-202 was launched by a Saturn IB rocket on August 25, 1966.
AS-202 was the first flight to test the Apollo command and service module’s guidance, navigation control system.
AS-202 was the first flight to test the Apollo command and service module’s fuel cells.
AS-202 proved the readiness of Block I hardware for crewed missions.
The mission goal of AS-202 was to test the Apollo spacecraft's systems in a high-heat re-entry environment.
Spacecraft 011 was used in AS-202.
The launch vehicle for AS-202 was Saturn IB (AS-202).
The launch site for AS-202 was Cape Kennedy, Launch Complex 34.
The flight duration of AS-202 was approximately 1 hour and 33 minutes.
AS-202 reached an altitude of over 660660660 nautical miles.
The command module of AS-202 re-entered the atmosphere.
The command module of AS-202 was successfully recovered in the Pacific Ocean.
NASA decided to officially skip the numbers 2 and 3 for named missions following the Apollo 1 fire.
The next crewed flight after the decision was designated Apollo 4.
AS-202 was uncrewed.
AS-203 was uncrewed.
AS-202 and AS-203 are often considered the unofficial Apollo 2 and 3.
A 1963 NASA report mentions an Apollo 2 in the context of a Second Generation Lunar Exploration System.
The 1963 NASA report proposes a direct-landing cargo/lunar landing vehicle.
